Upadeśa 4 (pratyāhāra) is numbered after the Vasu edition e-text (eBhāratī, śrīśchandra-vasu), since the Tirupati e-text lacks it. Thomi's edition (GRETIL) numbers some verses differently.

paraphrase: When by the practice of khecarī the tongue goes upward, success in samādhi comes, leaving ordinary activity. Performing the bhrāmarī retention with slow breath and exhaling very slowly, the sound of a bee arises; hearing the bee-sound within one leads the mind there; samādhi arises there, and bliss: 'I am He' (so'ham).
notes: Ref per Gheraṇḍasaṃhitā, eBhāratī-Sampat e-text (Rāṣṭriya Saṃskṛta Vidyāpīṭha, Tirupati; Ebharati-3860); numbering of that e-text. Upadeśa 4 (pratyāhāra) is numbered after the Vasu edition e-text (eBhāratī, śrīśchandra-vasu), since the Tirupati e-text lacks it. Thomi's edition (GRETIL) numbers some verses differently.

paraphrase: Performing yoni mudrā one becomes oneself full of the power and, with the sentiment of love, delights in the supreme self; becoming full of bliss one attains oneness with Brahman — 'I am Brahman' — and non-dual samādhi arises from it.
notes: Ref per Gheraṇḍasaṃhitā, eBhāratī-Sampat e-text (Rāṣṭriya Saṃskṛta Vidyāpīṭha, Tirupati; Ebharati-3860); numbering of that e-text. Upadeśa 4 (pratyāhāra) is numbered after the Vasu edition e-text (eBhāratī, śrīśchandra-vasu), since the Tirupati e-text lacks it. Thomi's edition (GRETIL) numbers some verses differently.

paraphrase: Attaining the swoon of the mind (manomūrcchā) one joins the mind to the self; from union with the supreme self one attains samādhi.
notes: Ref per Gheraṇḍasaṃhitā, eBhāratī-Sampat e-text (Rāṣṭriya Saṃskṛta Vidyāpīṭha, Tirupati; Ebharati-3860); numbering of that e-text. Upadeśa 4 (pratyāhāra) is numbered after the Vasu edition e-text (eBhāratī, śrīśchandra-vasu), since the Tirupati e-text lacks it. Thomi's edition (GRETIL) numbers some verses differently.

paraphrase: In a fine hut, seated on a seat in padmāsana, the yogin should practise the breath; with body straight and hands joined he bows to the gurus, to Gaṇeśa on the right and to Kṣetrapāla and Ambikā on the left; closing piṅgalā with the right thumb he fills through iḍā and holds as far as able, releases slowly through piṅgalā, then fills through piṅgalā, holds and releases slowly through iḍā; he does this at dawn, midday, sunset and midnight (with a stated number of retentions, not reproduced), free of sloth, for three months; then the channels are surely purified.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: When the channels are purified the signs appear in the yogin's body: an even body, fragrance, beauty, mastery of voice. The stages in all yogas are ārambha, ghaṭa, paricaya and niṣpatti. In the beginning stage the fire is strong, he enjoys well, is happy and handsome in all limbs, his heart full, endowed with all energy and strength.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: Now the things that obstruct yoga, which the yogin must give up: sour, astringent, pungent, salty, mustard and bitter food; much wandering, early-morning bathing, oil and burning; theft, violence, hatred of people, egotism and crookedness; fasting, untruth, harming beings; company of women, tending fire, much talk, likes and dislikes, and overeating.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: The means to quick success, to be kept secret: ghee, milk, sweet food, betel without lime, camphor, husked grains; a pleasant hut with a small opening; always hearing the doctrine, a dwelling of dispassion, singing the names of Viṣṇu, listening to fine sound; fortitude, patience, austerity, purity, modesty, faith and service of the guru — these the yogin should always observe.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: The wise do not practise immediately after eating nor when hungry; in the first period of practice one should take milk and ghee; when the practice is firm such restriction is not needed; the practitioner should eat a little at a time, several times.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: At the first effort sweat arises in the yogin's body; when it arises he should rub it in, otherwise the bodily element is lost. In the second (grade) there is trembling, in the middle the frog-like hopping (dārdurī); with still more practice he moves in the sky: the yogin, even seated in padmāsana, leaves the ground — then mastery of breath is known. Sleep, faeces and urine become slight; he is free of disease and dejection; sweat, saliva and worms do not arise; there is no restriction on food; eating little many times he is not troubled; by practice he attains the power of moving on the earth, as frogs move when struck by the hand.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: Many terrible obstacles, hard to ward off, arise here; still the yogin should persevere, even with his life in his throat. Seated in seclusion, senses controlled, the practitioner should repeat the praṇava, drawn out, to destroy the obstacles.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: When the ghaṭa stage arises in the practice of the breath, there is nothing in the wheel of saṃsāra he cannot achieve. Because prāṇa and apāna, nāda and bindu, the jīvātman and the paramātman meet (ghaṭate) together, it is called ghaṭa. When he is able to hold the breath for a long time (the text states a period, not reproduced), then there is pratyāhāra: whatever the yogin knows he should regard as the self; with whatever senses and in whatever way, he conquers those senses.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: Then by practice the paricaya stage comes: the breath, leaving sun and moon, stays motionless and moves in the space of the suṣumnā; taking the power of action it pierces the centres; in paricaya the yogin sees the three peaks of karma.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: At this time the great yogin should practise the fivefold concentration (dhāraṇā), by which mastery over earth and the other elements comes and fear of the elements is removed: (holding the breath) at the base, at the place of the liṅga, above that, at the navel-heart region, and above the brows (for periods the text states); the wise one who practises the concentration of all the elements has no death even after a hundred deaths of Brahmā.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: Then by practice the completion (niṣpatti) of the yogin comes, by which, crossing the seeds of beginningless karma, he drinks the nectar; when completion arises and samādhi comes by his own doing, it belongs to the calm, steadfast yogin liberated while living.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: Practices of 'drinking the breath' for removing afflictions: placing the tongue at the root of the palate and drinking the breath; drinking cool air through the crow's-beak mouth (with knowledge of prāṇa and apāna); pressing the cavity at the root of the front teeth; drinking with the teeth pressed together and the tongue upward. The text claims these destroy fatigue, burning, old age and disease, that with the tongue upward drinking the moon's water one conquers death in a month, and that after long practice one becomes like Bhairava, gains the powers such as aṇimā and is not stained by merit or sin.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: There are eighty-four postures of many kinds; from them four have been taken and are taught: siddhāsana, then padmāsana, the fierce posture (ugra) and svastika.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: Siddhāsana: pressing the perineum carefully with the heel and placing the other heel above the penis, gazing upward between the brows, motionless, senses restrained; by practising it one quickly reaches completion in yoga; the breath-practitioner should always use it; there is no posture more secret on earth, and by merely contemplating it the yogin is freed from sin.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: Padmāsana: the feet placed soles-up on the thighs, the hands palms-up between the thighs, the gaze on the nose-tip, the tongue at the root of the teeth, the chin raised (or set) on the chest, drawing in the breath slowly; it destroys all diseases and is obtained only by the wise; when it is done the breath at once moves evenly; the yogin in padmāsana who fills (with breath) by the method of prāṇa and apāna is liberated.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: The fierce posture (ugrāsana): stretching both legs apart without touching, holding them firmly with the hands and placing the head on the knees — this kindles the breath, removes bodily decline and is called paścimottāna; for one who practises it daily the breath moves by the back path; all success comes to its practitioners; it is to be kept secret.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: Svastika: holding both soles properly between the knees and thighs, the body straight, sitting comfortably; by it the wise yogin masters the breath and no disease enters the body; it is called the comfortable posture (sukhāsana), removing all pain; svastika, the best of auspicious things, is to be kept secret by yogins.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: Yoni mudrā: first by inhalation one fills the base (ādhāra) with the mind and contracts the yoni between the anus and the genitals; one meditates on Kāma in the brahma-yoni, like a ball, bright as millions of suns and cool as millions of moons, above it a subtle flame of consciousness, which goes by the path of Brahman through the three liṅgas to the nectar in heaven and returns to the kula by the measured yoga. By this binding there is nothing that cannot be accomplished: even mantras that are 'cut', 'nailed', 'paralysed', 'burnt' or otherwise defective become effective; one bound by yoni mudrā is not stained by the killing of a thousand brahmins, of the guru, drinking liquor, theft or the violation of the guru's bed. It is to be practised daily by those seeking liberation and not given to anyone even at the cost of life.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text. The praise of its sin-removing power is an arthavāda in the text's own manner.

paraphrase: Mahāmudrā, mahābandha, mahāvedha, khecarī, jālandhara, mūlabandha, viparītakaraṇī, uḍḍāna, vajrolī and, tenth, śakticālana — these are the ten mudrās.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text. The Muktabodha e-text names 'vajroṇī' in the list but has no vajrolī section; other editions include one.

paraphrase: Mahāmudrā, by which Kapila and the siddhas of old attained success: pressing the perineum with the left heel as the guru teaches, holding the stretched right leg with both hands, restraining the nine doors and placing the chin on the chest, setting the mind on the path of mind — this secret mahāmudrā is done on the left then the right side; by it even the unfortunate yogin succeeds; it moves all the channels, 'kills' bindu, revives the impure and destroys sins; it is to be kept secret, a wish-fulfilling cow for practitioners.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: Mahābandha: placing the stretched leg on the thigh, contracting the anus and yoni, making apāna go upward and joining it with samāna, turning prāṇa downward, one binds (them) for the upward movement; by practice the breath goes into the middle of the suṣumnā, the body is nourished, the skeleton firmly bound and the heart full; it is to be done with both legs.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: Mahāvedha: having united apāna and prāṇa and filled the belly with breath, one seated in mahāvedha gently strikes the buttocks; by this piercing, with the breath, the yogin pierces the brahma-knot through the path of the suṣumnā; the gods in the centres tremble at the striking of the breath and kuṇḍalinī, the great māyā, dissolves in Kailāsa. Mahāmudrā and mahābandha are fruitless without mahāvedha, so the yogin performs all three in order; the siddha alone knows their greatness; they are to be kept secret, for otherwise there is no success in the mudrās.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: RESTRICTED — summary only: khecarī is described as sitting in vajrāsana with the gaze firmly between the brows and joining the tongue, turned back, to the cavity above the uvula, the 'well of nectar'; the text says it is the mother of powers, that by it one drinks nectar daily and gains bodily perfection, that the one whose khecarī is pure is pure whatever his state, and that it is to be given to no one. The preparatory procedure is not reproduced.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: Jālandhara: binding the network of channels at the throat, placing the chin on the chest — hard even for the gods. The fire at the navel of creatures drinks the nectar falling from the thousand-petalled lotus; to prevent this one binds this lock, and by it the wise one drinks the nectar himself and, gaining immortality, rejoices in the three worlds.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: Mūlabandha: pressing the anal passage well with the heel and forcibly drawing up apāna, moving it gradually upward — this destroys old age and death; it unites apāna and prāṇa, and by it yoni mudrā succeeds; by its grace the yogin, seated in padmāsana, leaves the ground; it is to be practised in a well-hidden, solitary place by one who would cross the ocean of saṃsāra.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: Viparītakaraṇī: placing the head on the ground and raising the two feet into the air — secret in all the tantras; one who practises it daily for a watch conquers death, does not perish even at the dissolution, drinks the nectar and becomes equal to the siddhas.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: Uḍḍiyāna: drawing the belly back above and below the navel — this lock removes all sorrow, the lion to the elephant of death; practised daily (at stated times) the navel is purified, the breath is mastered, the fire in the belly blazes and the vital fluid increases; in six months one conquers death; the body is perfected and diseases destroyed; it is to be learned from the guru and practised in a solitary place.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: RESTRICTED — summary only: śakticālana is described as moving the kuṇḍalī asleep in the base lotus by forcibly drawing up apāna; the text says that by daily practice life is lengthened and diseases destroyed, the serpent leaves sleep and rises of herself, and success comes to one who practises it by the guru's instruction; the duration and procedure are not reproduced.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: Obstacles to liberation are of three kinds. Obstacles of enjoyment: women, beds, seats, clothes, wealth, betel, food, vehicles, kingdom and lordship, gold, silver, jewels, learning in the Vedas and śāstras, dance, song, ornaments and musical instruments, elephants and horses, wife, children and objects. Obstacles of religion (dharma): bathing, worship, fire-offering, vows, fasts, rules, silence, sense-restraint, the object and act of meditation, mantra, gifts, fame, building wells, tanks, temples and gardens, sacrifices, the cāndrāyaṇa and kṛcchra penances and the various pilgrimages. Obstacles of knowledge: (practices such as) sitting in gomukha, washing by dhauti, knowledge of the movement of the channels, the restraint of withdrawal, stirring the belly, and other techniques taken as knowledge.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text. The list of 'obstacles of knowledge' (5.5-8) is obscure in the e-text; paraphrased cautiously.

paraphrase: Practitioners are of four kinds — mild, middling, strong and very strong; the very strong is best, able to cross the ocean of becoming. The mild (lacking zeal, sickly, faulting the guru, greedy, dependent) is fit for mantra-yoga and succeeds in twelve years; the middling (even-minded, patient, seeking merit, sweet-spoken) is given laya-yoga; the strong (steady, independent, brave, compassionate, devoted to the guru's feet) is given haṭha-yoga with its limbs and succeeds in six years; the very strong, fit for all yogas, succeeds in three years.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: Worship of one's image (pratīka): gazing with wide eyes at one's reflection-image in strong sunlight and then seeing one's image in the sky; seeing it daily lengthens life and there is no death; when one sees the whole image in the sky one conquers the breath and moves freely; by its grace one worships the supreme, the one Person full of bliss; it is to be done at the time of a journey, a wedding, an auspicious act, in danger, for the destruction of sin and increase of merit.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: Closing both ears with the thumbs, the eyes with the index fingers, the nostrils with the middle fingers and the mouth firmly with the ring fingers, restraining the breath, the yogin sees the self as light; whoever sees that light even for a moment is freed of all sins and reaches the supreme goal; by constant practice he forgets the body and becomes one with it; practised secretly it merges one in Brahman; this yoga, dear to Śiva, gives immediate conviction; then the nāda arises gradually.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: The first sound is like that of intoxicated bees, flute and vīṇā; then, by practice, a sound like a bell and then like the rumble of clouds, which destroys the darkness of saṃsāra; when one sets the mind on that sound and stays fearless, laya arises; the mind delighting in nāda forgets everything outward and becomes still with the nāda; by this practice, having overcome the many qualities, abandoning all undertakings, one dissolves in the space of consciousness.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: There is no posture like siddha, no power like retention, no mudrā like khecarī and no dissolution like nāda.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: Seated in padmāsana, recollecting the pit of the throat and placing the tongue at the root of the palate, the yogin's hunger and thirst cease; below the pit of the throat is the lovely kūrma-channel; fixing the mind there he gains great steadiness of mind.
notes: Ref per Śivasaṃhitā, Muktabodha e-text M00082 (Varanasi 1928 printing); numbering of that e-text — other editions (e.g. Vasu; Mallinson 2007) number differently and include a vajrolī section absent from this e-text.

paraphrase: Laya-yoga is the dissolution of mind, brought about by the 'signals' (saṅketa), of which Ādinātha taught eight crore: meditating on the void day and night while standing, walking, sleeping and eating; merely gazing at the nose-tip; meditating on the back of the head, which conquers death; gazing between the brows; (attending to) the forehead and the brows; dissolution on the big toes of the right and left feet; lying on the ground like a corpse, relaxed in a solitary place — whatever signal dissolves one's mind is laya-yoga.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: Yama, niyama, posture, breath-control, withdrawal, concentration, meditation and samādhi — this eight-limbed yoga is known to Yājñavalkya and others; Kapila and his followers practised haṭha as follows: mahāmudrā, mahābandha, khecarī mudrā, jālandhara, uḍḍiyāna, mūlabandha, viparītakaraṇī, and vajrolī — with amarolī and sahajolī, threefold.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: Among the eighty-four lakh postures the best, taught by Ādinātha: the feet placed soles-up on the thighs, the hands palms-up between the thighs, the gaze set on the nose-tip, the tongue at the root of the front teeth, the chin raised (to) the chest, the breath drawn in slowly as far as able to fill the belly and released slowly — this padmāsana destroys all diseases; it is hard to attain and only the wise obtain it.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: Young, old or sick, by gradual practice everyone who is not lazy attains success in yoga; whether brāhmaṇa, śramaṇa, Buddhist, Jain, Kāpālika or materialist, the wise one endowed with faith who practises yoga constantly attains all success.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: Success comes to one engaged in practice, not to the idle; no success comes from merely reading scripture; neither a shaven head nor a staff, ochre robes, talk of Nārāyaṇa, matted hair, smearing with ash, uttering 'namaḥ śivāya', outer worship or worship of the twelve places brings success to one without practice; garb is not the cause of success — practice alone is, truly.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently. In 42 the vulgate e-text reads kṛpaiva ('grace alone'), evidently for kriyaiva ('practice alone'), as HYP 1.66 has it.

paraphrase: Those who wear the garb and talk of yoga for the sake of belly and genitals, without practice, deceive people; deluded, given to enjoyment, they strive with high-sounding deceptions saying 'we are yogins'; recognising such garb-wearers who shun practice, one should avoid them — they are always obstacles to the practice of yoga.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: At the first practice the obstacles are: first sloth, second boasting, third the company of rogues and the pursuit of mantras, fourth alchemy (dhātuvāda), fifth theories about food (khādyavāda); many such are seen, like mirages; the wise, knowing them, should give them up.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: Then, seated in padmāsana, one should practise breath-control in a pleasant hut with a small door and no cracks, well smeared with cow-dung or lime, carefully kept free of bugs, mosquitoes and creatures, swept daily, perfumed and fumigated with guggulu and the like, on a seat of cloth or skin spread out, not touching others.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: Seated in padmāsana with body straight and hands joined, bowing to one's chosen deity, one closes piṅgalā with the right thumb and fills slowly through iḍā, holds as far as able, releases slowly through piṅgalā, then fills through piṅgalā and releases (through iḍā) — this is sahita retention, with inhalation and exhalation; it is done at dawn, midday, evening and midnight (with a stated number each time, not reproduced), without sloth, for three months; then the channels are purified.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: When the channels are purified outward signs appear in the yogin's body: lightness of body, radiance, increase of the digestive fire and slimness.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: Things obstructing yoga to be avoided: salt, mustard, sour, hot, dry and sharp food; overeating; union with women; tending the fire; the company of rogues. The means to quick success: ghee, milk, sweet food and moderate diet.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: Practising the breath at the times stated, one gains the power to hold the breath at will; from holding it at will kevala retention is attained; when kevala retention, free of exhalation and inhalation, is attained, nothing in the three worlds is hard to obtain.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: First sweat arises — one should rub it in; then by holding the breath further, gradually, trembling arises in the body of the seated yogin; with more practice the frog-like hopping (dardurī): as a frog goes leaping on the ground, so goes the yogin seated in padmāsana; with still more practice he leaves the ground and, still in padmāsana, stays without support; little urine, faeces and sleep; worms, rheum, saliva, sweat and bad smell no longer arise; great strength comes by which he gains mastery of those who move on earth — tigers, buffaloes, wild oxen, elephants or lions die at a slap of his hand — and he becomes beautiful as the god of love.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: At that time a great obstacle arises through carelessness: women, captivated by his beauty, desire union with him; if he unites with them his bindu is lost; from the loss of bindu, life shortens and weakness arises; so bindu is to be guarded with every effort. Then, seated in seclusion, he should repeat the praṇava with prolonged measure to destroy past sins; the praṇava removes all obstacles and all faults.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: Thus the success of the beginning stage arises from practice; then comes the ghaṭa stage: when prāṇa and apāna, mind and breath, the individual self and the supreme self join without opposition, that is known as the ghaṭa stage of yogins.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: Giving up the fourfold (daily) practice described earlier, one should do kevala retention once a day (for a period the text states). Withdrawing the senses clearly from their objects while holding the retention is called pratyāhāra: whatever one sees with the eyes, one should contemplate as the self; whatever one smells, as the self; so with all the senses of knowledge. Then wondrous powers surely arise: far-hearing, far-seeing, going far in a moment, perfection of speech, going where one wishes, invisibility, turning iron and other metals to gold by smearing them with one's excreta, and moving in the sky.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: Then the wise yogin should reflect: these (powers) are obstacles to the great success, and the wise does not delight in them. He should never display his powers to anyone, except perhaps out of affection to one who is devoted; he should move in the world like a fool, a dullard or a deaf man to hide his powers; otherwise many disciples come, and, busy with their affairs, he forgets his own practice and, without practice, becomes worldly. Not forgetting the guru's words he should practise day and night.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: Then by practice the paricaya stage arises: the breath, driven with effort, awakens kuṇḍalinī together with the fire and enters the suṣumnā without obstruction; with the breath the mind enters the great path — the great path, the cremation ground, the suṣumnā.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: The fivefold concentration, removing fear of each element: holding the breath (for a stated period) below the navel and above the anus is earth-concentration — he does not die of earth; at the navel, water — no fear or death from water; above the navel, fire — he does not die by fire and is not burnt even when thrown into a fire-pit; in the three regions between navel and brows, air — no fear from wind; above the brows, space — he conquers death and is happy wherever he is; practising the five, the body becomes firm and there is no death even at Brahmā's dissolution.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently. Durations (ghaṭikās) not reproduced.

paraphrase: Now the view of the siddhas such as Kapila (the haṭha of mudrās); the difference lies in practice, the fruit is the same. Mahāmudrā, taught by Bhairava: place the left heel at the perineum, stretch out the right leg and hold it firmly with the hands, set the chin on the chest, fill with breath, hold as able and release, on the left then the right side. Placing the stretched leg on the thigh is mahābandha; seated in it one gently strikes the buttocks (the vulgate calls this too mahābandha; it corresponds to mahāvedha).
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: Turning the tongue back and binding it within the cavity of the skull, with the gaze between the brows — this is khecarī mudrā.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: Contracting the throat and firmly setting (the chin) on the chest is jālandhara, which guards the flow of nectar: the fire at the navel always burns the nectar falling from the thousand-petalled lotus in the skull; by practice one drinks it oneself instead of the fire, and it goes by the back path and makes the body immortal; therefore practise jālandhara.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: Uḍḍiyāna, declared natural by the guru, practised without sloth makes even the old young: drawing back above and below the navel with effort, practising for six months one conquers death. The one who daily practises mūlabandha, pressing the anus with the heel and contracting the breath forcibly again and again so that it rises, knows yoga; by mūlabandha prāṇa and apāna, nāda and bindu become one and give success in yoga.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: Viparītakaraṇī destroys all diseases; for its daily practitioner the digestive fire grows, so ample food must be provided — if food is scanty the fire burns (the body); sun above, moon below: head down and feet up for a moment on the first day, a little more each day; after six months wrinkles and grey hair are not seen; one who practises it daily for a watch knows yoga.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: RESTRICTED — summary only: vajrolī is kept secret by all yogins and is to be told only to one as dear as one's own life; even one who lives as he pleases without the yogic rules, if he knows vajrolī, is a vessel of success; it requires two things hard to obtain; man or woman may succeed in it by pursuing their own aim; bindu that moves is drawn back up and guarded; death comes from the fall of bindu, life from holding it, and by the grace of guarding bindu everything succeeds. The procedure is not reproduced.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: RESTRICTED — summary only: amarolī and sahajolī are to be practised in the order handed down in the siddhas' tradition; practising these for a long time rājayoga follows — success comes only by practice, not by mere pointing.
notes: Ref per Dattātreyayogaśāstra, vulgate of 154 verses (sanskritdocuments.org / eBhāratī e-text); Mallinson's critical edition numbers differently.

paraphrase: The yogin who knows mahāmudrā, nabhomudrā, uḍḍiyāna, jālandhara and mūlabandha is a vessel of success.
notes: Ref per Gorakṣaśataka, GRETIL e-text of the Kuvalayananda–Shukla edition (Lonavla).

paraphrase: With the chin on the chest, pressing the perineum long with the left foot, holding the outstretched right leg with the hands, filling both sides of the belly with breath and binding it, one should exhale slowly — this is the very great mudrā, destroyer of sins.
notes: Ref per Gorakṣaśataka, GRETIL e-text of the Kuvalayananda–Shukla edition (Lonavla).

paraphrase: When the tongue, turned back, enters the cavity of the skull and the gaze is between the brows, that is khecarī mudrā.
notes: Ref per Gorakṣaśataka, GRETIL e-text of the Kuvalayananda–Shukla edition (Lonavla).

paraphrase: Above the penis and below the navel is uḍḍiyāna, the lock that conquers — the lion to the elephant of death; when jālandhara, marked by contraction of the throat, is made, the nectar does not fall into the fire and the breath is not disturbed; pressing the perineum with the heel, contracting the anus and drawing apāna upward is called mūlabandha.
notes: Ref per Gorakṣaśataka, GRETIL e-text of the Kuvalayananda–Shukla edition (Lonavla).

paraphrase: In bound padmāsana, having bowed to the guru Śiva, alone, with the gaze at the nose-tip, the yogin should practise breath-control: fill through the moon, hold as able, release through the sun, meditating on the moon-disc white as the ocean of milk, full of nectar; draw in through the sun, fill the belly slowly, hold by rule and release through the moon, meditating on the blazing disc of the sun at the navel — and he is happy in breath-control.
notes: Ref per Gorakṣaśataka, GRETIL e-text of the Kuvalayananda–Shukla edition (Lonavla).

paraphrase: In the lowest (grade) there is heavy sweat, in the middle trembling, in the highest the yogin in bound padmāsana rises up again and again; rubbing the limbs with the water born of the effort is recommended; giving up pungent, sour and salty food, one should take milk.
notes: Ref per Gorakṣaśataka, GRETIL e-text of the Kuvalayananda–Shukla edition (Lonavla).

paraphrase: One should draw in the breath slowly and release it slowly; one should not hold the breath excessively nor release it quickly.
notes: Ref per Gorakṣaśataka, GRETIL e-text of the Kuvalayananda–Shukla edition (Lonavla).

paraphrase: By posture the yogin destroys disease, by breath-control sin, and by withdrawal disturbance of mind.
notes: Ref per Gorakṣaśataka, GRETIL e-text of the Kuvalayananda–Shukla edition (Lonavla).

paraphrase: The sun draws in (pratyāharati) the stream of nectar from the moon — that drawing-in is called pratyāhāra. The sun at the navel is burning; the moon at the root of the palate is made of nectar; the moon, facing down, rains, and the sun, facing up, swallows; the technique by which the nectar is obtained must be known.
notes: Ref per Gorakṣaśataka, GRETIL e-text of the Kuvalayananda–Shukla edition (Lonavla).

paraphrase: Navel above and palate below, sun above and moon below — the technique called viparīta is obtained from the guru's mouth.
notes: Ref per Gorakṣaśataka, GRETIL e-text of the Kuvalayananda–Shukla edition (Lonavla).

paraphrase: In the heart one practises concentration on the five elements separately, with the mind unmoving: earth — yellow as orpiment, with la, four-cornered, with Brahmā, in the heart; water — white as the half-moon or jasmine, in the throat, with va and Viṣṇu; fire — like the indragopa insect, triangular, at the palate, with ra and Rudra; air — like a heap of collyrium, round, between the brows, with ya and Īśvara; space — like pure water, in the brahmarandhra, with ha and Sadāśiva — in each the breath is held with the mind (for a period stated); they are called the stabilising, liquefying, burning, whirling and drying concentrations of the elements; these five, hard to master in act, mind and word, free the yogin from all sins.
notes: Ref per Gorakṣaśataka, GRETIL e-text of the Kuvalayananda–Shukla edition (Lonavla).

paraphrase: The breath goes out with the sound 'ha' and enters again with 'sa'; the jīva always repeats this mantra 'haṃsa haṃsa', twenty-one thousand six hundred times in a day and night; this is the gāyatrī called ajapā, which gives yogins liberation; by merely resolving on it one is freed from all sins; there is no knowledge, repetition or wisdom equal to it; this gāyatrī arises from kuṇḍalinī and sustains life — the one who knows this science of the breath knows yoga.
notes: Ref per Gorakṣaśataka in the recension printed by Briggs (Muktabodha e-text M00522); numbering of that e-text.

paraphrase: Śiva teaches a proof as sweet as nectar that gives immediate conviction: the unstruck sound in ten forms — first 'ciṇī', second 'ciñciṇī', third 'ciri', fourth the conch, fifth the sound of strings, sixth a ringing, seventh bronze cymbals, eighth the cloud, ninth the roar of water and tenth the kettle-drum; abandoning the nine, the tenth gives liberation; without striking, nāda makes this tenfold sound, emerging in the opening of the ear.
notes: Ref per Nādānusandhāna (Śiva–Devī dialogue), Muktabodha e-text M00526 (NGMCP A62/11) and eBhāratī e-text Ebharati-11931. The e-texts are faulty in places; the list is read from the Muktabodha/eBhāratī e-texts.

paraphrase: The sounds are correlated with the elements and their maṇḍalas: the 'ciṇī' sound with earth, square and yellow, giving freedom from cold and disease; the conch and related sounds with water in its crescent; the flute-like sounds with fire in its triangle; the bronze and cloud sounds with air in its hexagon; the kettle-drum with space; attention through them brings the dissolution of the principles in order.
notes: Ref per Nādānusandhāna (Śiva–Devī dialogue), Muktabodha e-text M00526 (NGMCP A62/11) and eBhāratī e-text Ebharati-11931. Reconstructed from a corrupt e-text; low confidence in details.

paraphrase: The mudrās beginning with āvāhanī delight all the deities: the añjali filled with flowers is āvāhanī (invitation); the same turned downward is for installing (sthāpana); the two fists joined with thumbs raised is sannidhāna (making present); the same with the thumbs inside is sannirodha (holding there); the two fists turned upward is sammukhīkaraṇa (turning to face); placing the six limbs on the deity's body is sakalīkaraṇa.
notes: Muktabodha e-text M00077 with Rāghavabhaṭṭa's Padārthādarśa; numbering of that e-text.

paraphrase: Avaguṇṭhana: a fist of the right hand with the index finger extended downward, rotated around. Dhenu: the little and ring fingers, and the index and middle fingers, of the two hands joined facing each other — with it the teacher performs amṛtīkaraṇa (making nectar). Mahāmudrā: the thumbs interlocked and the fingers extended — used for paramīkaraṇa in the worship of the deity.

Rāghavabhaṭṭa's commentary: mudrā is so called because it gives joy (mudaṃ rāti) to the deities; the fingers from little finger to thumb are earth, water, fire, air and space, and their mutual joining makes the deity present; the mudrās are not to be shown in a crowd or to the uninitiated, lest the deities be disturbed and the rite fruitless; for seekers of liberation the mudrās may be made mentally.
notes: Commentary (Padārthādarśa) quoting other tantras; recorded here under the root text's id with /comm.
